attacks.claim: Partner-chosen filenames are interpolated unquoted into a shell=True gsutil command. A filename containing spaces, quotes, or shell metacharacters (e.g. `;`, `$()`) will break the command or execute arbitrary commands on a worker that holds write credentials for the whole raw bucket.
attacks.evidence: subprocess.run(f"gsutil -q ... cp {local} {dest}", shell=True, check=True) — and partners "choose their own filenames"; dest embeds src.stem

attacks.claim: Partition date changed from UTC to local time while the job runs in America/Los_Angeles, and the scheduler fires at 01:30 UTC. Locally that is 17:30 or 18:30 the previous day, so the dt partition written is the wrong day and dashboards reading the UTC dt partition get data under the wrong date or miss it.
attacks.evidence: def partition_date() -> str: return datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d")  (was datetime.now(timezone.utc)); context: TZ=America/Los_Angeles, scheduled 01:30 UTC, dt=YYYY-MM-DD UTC date

attacks.claim: Per-file failures are swallowed and the _SUCCESS marker is written unconditionally, so a partially or fully failed partner run publishes a success signal that dashboards read immediately. Partial data is silently treated as complete.
attacks.evidence: except Exception: log.exception(...); failed += 1  ... write_success_marker(BUCKET, f"raw/{partner}/dt={dt}/") with no check that failed == 0

attacks.claim: Failed uploads leave orphan chunk files in work_dir and partial objects in GCS; the chunk unlink only runs on success, and a mid-file failure leaves earlier chunks uploaded under the same dt with no cleanup or retry, so reruns can produce duplicate or mixed partial data.
attacks.evidence: for chunk in _write_chunks(src, work_dir): _upload(chunk, ...); chunk.unlink()  — no try/finally, no cleanup of already-uploaded chunks

attacks.claim: Chunk-level schema can drift: the DictWriter fieldnames are taken from the first normalised row of each chunk, so a row whose normalised keys differ will raise or misalign columns, and each chunk header is independent, making downstream multi-file reads inconsistent.
attacks.evidence: if writer is None: writer = csv.DictWriter(out, fieldnames=list(norm.keys())); writer.writeheader()

attacks.claim: Gzip chunk filenames use src.stem and a chunk index, but the object path also includes src_name, so the chunk uniqueness depends on stem collisions between differently-extensioned files; also work_dir is not guaranteed to be cleaned on exception.
attacks.evidence: path = out_dir / f"{src.stem}-{len(chunks):04d}.csv.gz"; dest = f"gs://{BUCKET}/raw/{partner}/dt={dt}/{src_name}/{local.name}"

attacks.claim: The PR asserts parallel composite uploads are much faster than the client library and that streaming fixes the OOM, but no benchmark or memory measurement is provided. Also, the parallel composite threshold is set to 150M, while chunks of 500k rows are likely far smaller, so the optimisation may never trigger.
attacks.evidence: "parallel composite uploads are much faster than the client library for multi-GB objects"; CHUNK_ROWS = 500_000 with threshold parallel_composite_upload_threshold=150M

attacks.claim: The change drops the storage client dependency and moves to a subprocess to an external binary, adding an undeclared runtime dependency on gsutil being installed and authenticated on workers.
attacks.evidence: import subprocess ... gsutil -q -o ... cp (no client; import of google.cloud.storage removed)

attacks.claim: Changing partition path structure to add src_name directory level and changing the partition date basis alters the on-disk layout that downstream consumers read, with no migration or compatibility note.

attacks.claim: Chunks are written sequentially and uploaded inline, so one slow gsutil call blocks the entire partner run; there is no concurrency across files and no bound on local disk used in work_dir beyond per-chunk unlink on success.

attacks.claim: partition_date() now uses naive local time. Workers run with TZ=America/Los_Angeles and the job starts at 01:30 UTC (about 17:30 PT the previous day), so rows land in the previous day's dt partition. This contradicts the stated requirement that dashboards read a UTC-date partition.
attacks.evidence: def partition_date() -> str: return datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d") (previously datetime.now(timezone.utc)); context: "TZ=America/Los_Angeles", "scheduled at 01:30 UTC", "dt=YYYY-MM-DD partition (UTC date)"

attacks.claim: Failure leaves partial state behind: chunks already uploaded for a failed file stay in GCS, and local chunks are not unlinked on exception. Reruns use deterministic names, so a rerun that produces fewer chunks leaves stale chunk objects in the same dt prefix, duplicating or mixing data. Cleanup/rollback is not defined.
attacks.evidence: for chunk in _write_chunks(...): _upload(...); chunk.unlink()  (no cleanup in except branch); object name f"{src.stem}-{len(chunks):04d}.csv.gz"

attacks.claim: Failures are only logged and counted. The run exits 0 and nothing alerts, so a partner with failed files looks healthy in ops. The count is not exposed as a metric or a non-zero exit code.
attacks.evidence: log.info("partner=%s dt=%s ok=%d failed=%d", partner, dt, ok, failed)  (no raise, no exit code, no metric)

attacks.claim: The CSV header is taken from the first normalised row of each chunk, and DictWriter raises on any later row with different keys. attacks.claim: Parsing semantics changed from pandas to csv: short rows yield None values, extra fields go under a None key, blank lines and NA handling differ.
